senseForms.note: the plural forms: diese Bücher, mit diesen Kindern

profile.feeling: Pointing: this one here (or that one there) – clearer than the article.

senses.def: this (also “that” when nothing is contrasted) – points to a particular thing: dieser Tisch, diese Lampe, dieses Buch
dieser / diese / dieses alone: this one
these (plural diese, for all genders): diese Bücher, diese Kinder

examples.text: Welche Gurke willst du? – Diese hier.
examples.tr: Which cucumber do you want? – This one here.

synonyms.nuance: in speech the stressed article often replaces dieser: DIE Tomate (da)
that (far) – old-fashioned and written; contrasted with dieser

etymology.text: Inherited from Middle High German diser/dirre, disiu, diz, from Old High German dësēr, disiu, diz, from the Old High German demonstrative pronoun dër, from Proto-Germanic *sa, from Proto-Indo-European *tód.

funFacts: dieser has the same endings as der in all cases – -er, -e, -es, -en, -em – which is why it is often used to learn the article endings.
pitfalls: Neuter is dieses (dieses Radieschen), not *dieser; the short form dies is used mostly as a pronoun in writing (Dies ist …).
Plural diese for every gender: dieser Mann → diese Männer, dieses Kind → diese Kinder.
subtleties: German does not distinguish this/that sharply: dieser covers both; in speech people often say der da or das hier.

senseForms.none: every meaning uses the same forms

profile.feeling: The pointing word of “Das ist …” – used for anything you show or name.

senses.def: this, that (demonstrative pronoun): Das ist eine Tomate. Das sind Tomaten.
that (referring to a whole statement): Das weiß ich nicht.
that (pointing farther away; in speech often das da): Das da ist mein Haus.

examples.tr: Is that your key over there?

synonyms.nuance: short form of dieses; Dies ist … sounds written or formal

etymology.text: From Middle High German daȥ, from Old High German daȥ, from Proto-Germanic *þat. Compare Dutch dat, English that. Doublet of dass.

funFacts: das and dass (“that”, conjunction) are historically the same word; the spelling difference is only a convention.
pitfalls: In Das ist … the das never changes with the noun: Das ist ein Kürbis / eine Gurke / ein Radieschen; for plurals the verb changes: Das sind Gurken.
subtleties: This das is the neuter form of the demonstrative der/die/das; its dative is dem and its genitive dessen (not des).
Das ist … covers both “this is” and “that is”; add hier or da/dort when the distance matters: Das hier ist … / Das da ist …

contrasts.value: at this place, where the speaker is

profile.feeling: Right here, within reach – presence and attention.

senses.def: here, at this point (in a text or discussion)
Hier! – “present!” (answer at roll call); also “here you are” when handing something

collocations.tr: here and there; now and then

phrases.meaning: in some places; from time to time

synonyms.nuance: in speech often means “here” as well as “there”: Ich bin da.
at this point – in writing and speeches

etymology.text: From Middle High German hier, from Old High German hier, from Proto-West Germanic *hēr. Cognate with Dutch hier, English here, Swedish här.

funFacts: In German schools and the army, pupils and soldiers answer the roll call with Hier!
pitfalls: For movement towards the speaker standard German uses her or hierher: Komm her! / Komm hierher!
subtleties: hier, da and dort: hier is close to the speaker, dort is far away, and da can be either.

senseForms.note: the plural forms: jene, die … (those who …)

profile.feeling: Distance in time or space – the written, slightly literary “that”.

senses.def: that (far from the speaker, or contrasted with dieser) – written or formal
those (plural jene); jene, die … = those who …
dieser … jener = the latter … the former (in careful writing)

examples.text: In jener Nacht konnte niemand schlafen.
Dieses Haus ist neu, jenes ist alt.
examples.tr: This house is new, that one is old.

examples.text: Jene, die zu spät kommen, müssen warten.
examples.tr: Those who come late have to wait.

collocations.tr: in those days, at that time
this one and that one; various people

synonyms.nuance: the spoken way to say that: der Tisch da, die Frau da
this – also used for “that” when no contrast is needed

etymology.text: From Middle High German jener, from Old High German jenēr, from Proto-West Germanic *jain, from Proto-Germanic *jainaz. Cognate with English yon.

funFacts: jener is the German cousin of English yon and yonder.
pitfalls: In everyday speech almost nobody says jener. Spoken German points with der/die/das + da: der Mann da (that man), das Buch da (that book), or simply dieser.
Same endings as dieser and der: jener, jene, jenes; jenen, jenem.
subtleties: dieser und jener (“this and that”) means “various people / things”: Ich habe mit diesem und jenem gesprochen.

contrasts.value: there – mentioned or pointed at, near or far
verb at the end; a reason already known, often at the start

profile.feeling: Pointing and presence: there – or simply “here, present”.

senses.def: there (at that place – pointing or already mentioned)
der/die/das … da – that … there (pointing at a person or thing)
since, as (because – at the start of a sentence: Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause)

examples.text: Das Buch liegt da, auf dem Tisch.
examples.tr: The book is there, on the table.

examples.text: Wir saßen beim Essen, da klingelte das Telefon.
examples.tr: We were having dinner when the phone rang.

examples.text: Ich wollte gerade gehen, da kam mein Chef herein.
examples.tr: I was just about to leave when my boss came in.

examples.text: Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause.
examples.tr: Since it is raining, we are staying at home.

examples.text: Da ich kein Auto habe, fahre ich mit dem Bus.
examples.tr: As I have no car, I take the bus.

collocations.tr: here and there; now and then
to be there, to be present

phrases.meaning: now we’re in a mess (what I feared has happened)
nothing can be done about it

synonyms.nuance: there – clearly away from the speaker, a little more precise and formal
over there, on the other side

etymology.text: From a merger of three interrelated adverbs: Middle High German dā, dār (“there, at that place”), from Old High German thār, dār, from Proto-West Germanic *þār; Middle High German dar, dare (“thither, to that place”); and Middle High German dō, duo (“then, at that time”), from Old High German thō, dō. Adverbs 1 and 2 are cognate with Dutch daar, Low German dar, dor.

funFacts: Heidegger built his philosophy on Dasein, “being there” – the ordinary German word for existence.
pitfalls: da can mean here! Ich bin da = I’m here / I’ve arrived. The situation decides.
For a direction use dahin / dorthin: Ich gehe dahin (not *Ich gehe da in standard writing).
subtleties: In speech, “that” is usually der/die/das + noun + da: Die Lampe da ist schön (That lamp is nice); “this” is … hier: die Lampe hier.
As a conjunction da means “since, as”: Da es regnet, bleiben wir zu Hause – a different use.

profile.feeling: Over there, away from us – precise, clear distance.

senses.def: there, over there (away from the speaker and the listener)

examples.tr: Do you see the house over there?

examples.text: Wir waren letztes Jahr in Wien und es war schön dort.
examples.tr: We were in Vienna last year and it was lovely there.

examples.text: Von dort aus kann man das Meer sehen.
examples.tr: From there you can see the sea.

synonyms.nuance: there (or here) – vaguer, the usual spoken word
over there, on the other side (of a street, a border)

etymology.text: From Middle High German dort, from Old High German doret, dārot (“thither”), from Proto-West Germanic *þārud (“thither”).

funFacts: dort first meant “to there, thither”; today the direction needs -hin: dorthin.
pitfalls: For movement towards the place use dorthin: Ich fahre morgen dorthin (not *Ich fahre morgen dort).
subtleties: dort is clear distance; da is vaguer and far more frequent in speech; hier is close to the speaker.
